blocks.x: See we're recording this in the Howard Tilton Library Seminar Room 2 and let's get your name down first. George Blanchin. And see today is November the...
The 12th isn't it? 13th. Friday the 13th. And where were you born? In New Orleans. And your birth date? March 1st, 1905. 1905.
Now you have a musical background, don't you? That's right, you told me. Your father.

Well that's correct. My father was a so-called legitimate musician. He studied and graduated from the Conservatory of Music in Paris, with very high honors and was considered a very fine musician. He played in the orchestras for his violinist at the old French Opera House. He conducted the orchestra at the Grunewald Cave, the Crescent and Tulane Theaters, which were legitimate theaters, the Dauphine Theater. That was before the Dauphine was burlesque. And of course he had many pupils in and around New Orleans, because he taught also. And of course my interest in music began when I was very young. I started studying violin at about the age of five. And became interested in jazz music not so very long afterwards, because I was hearing the Negro bands at the funerals and marching bands and whatnot. Much to the same displeasure of my father, who of course didn't like jazz and thought I should have no part of it.
What was the first band you remember hearing that played any jazz by name?

Well, that's rather difficult. When you say by name, I guess I would have to go to the bands I heard across the lake, which would have been bands such as Buddy Petit, Sam Morgan, Claiborne Williams, bands of that nature.
Are they all colored bands over there?

Well, just about all. I would say 95% of the bands that played for the dancers around Covington and Bogalusa and that section, where I spent my summers in those days, were colored bands. I recall, however, one white band, which was a band from Bogalusa, called Blanchard's Jazz Band. And the only musician I recall, and the only musician I recall in the band was Snoozer Quinn. I suppose I remember him more than the others because of his deformity. Anyone that ever saw Snoozer would never forget him. And I imagine that would date back to just around 19... 19, 1920. I've heard bands, jazz bands, before that, but don't recall the names or anyone connected with them.
What did Snoozer play like then?

Well, truthfully, my interest wasn't great enough at that time to actually say that he was a great musician then. Of course, I know later that he did become a very great musician. But at that time, I wouldn't have been qualified to judge him anyway, I don't suppose.
Well, what did he play like when you do remember him?

Well, the next I heard of Snoozer was when I worked for the old Al Grunewald Music Company, and Snoozer came in occasionally to have his instrument repaired or maybe to get some strings and whatnot, and he'd sit back in a booth and play. And I thought he was a very wonderful musician.
Did he sound anything like the records that Johnny put on?
Yes, I would say so, yes.
What did Buddy Petit look like, by the way?

Well, Buddy, as I recall, was on the small side, but had a very, very powerful tone. And Buddy played on the excursion boats running from West End to Mandeville and Lewisburg. I don't know what arrangement he had with the boat people, but I would imagine that they played for practically the cost of the trip going over there, so they could play a date that night either in Mandeville or Covington or one of the surrounding towns. And the thing I remember most vividly about Buddy was with this powerful tone, and being as small as he was, he looked very funny because when he'd blow his neck would puff out to such a great extent. He looked like a cobra. And it was said that, I don't know how true, but that one Buddy blasted out, if he was in the middle of the lake you could hear him from either side. I doubt that statement, but nevertheless he was to have a very powerful...
How did he compare with Sam Morgan?
When you say compare...
I meant for volume and...

Actually, I don't think I've ever heard anyone blow any louder than Buddy. He had a tremendous volume to his horn. I've heard better cornet players, I guess, but none that could play any louder. I would say this too, that in Sam Morgan's case, I think Sam Morgan, from my memory, had a better band than Buddy. But he had a pretty rough band, as I recall it. Not smooth at all.
Let me see now. Who else did you mention that you heard over there in those days?

Well, in those days, I'll tell you, one of the most sought-after bands in that part of the country was the Claven Williams Band, from Donisonville. I wish I could tell you more about it, but I can't, other than that it was very much in demand. And as I recall it, they had a rather large band. I think they used eight or ten pieces.
Would they be of the school of Pierron or more like Buddy Petit?
No, I would say more of the school of Pierron or possibly the old tuxedo bands of Celestan and Wrigley.
If you can give me the date on that, that would be good too.
Well, it was in the early 20s, that's about all I close to that.
Early 20s? And who were the people?

Well, the only musicians I recall with Buddy Petit at the time was Edmund Hall on clarinet and a George Washington on trombone. I think there have been several George Washington trombones. I can't tell you which one this was, but there was a George Washington on trombone. Short film? My memory's not good enough. I don't remember. Around the same time, I just mentioned two or three bands there, but there were bands such as, I believe, Silverleaf Band, the Tuxedo Band. And I'm quite sure that Punch Miller and Kid Ory and George Lewis and Bichet and all of those jazzmen played over there at some time or other, because it was quite a place for them to get work, and I think they enjoyed getting over there on weekends too. And I might mention this, might be of some interest, that if there were to be a dance, for instance, on a Saturday night, when the band got into town, and most of those small towns are usually a main street and a drugstore, and they would get either in front of the drugstore or maybe in front of the one theatre in the town and play for a half hour or so, publicizing the dance that night. In New Orleans here, as you know, they used to go around in the wagons to publicize the dances and prize fights and whatnot.
What did Buddy play in Mandeville? Would he play in a dance hall or in a pavilion?
No, he played in a pavilion, in most cases, called Jackson Park, which was on the outskirts of Mandeville.
Is that right on the lake? Right off the lake, yes. I think that's still standing, is it?

It may, possibly it is still there. In Covington, as an example, they would play at, well, there was a St. Tammany Fairgrounds, and of course, each year at the fair there would be dancing and orchestras. Then there was Vogue Folia Park, which is right near the center of Covington. Then there were also dances at the old Southern Hotel in Covington. In Bogalusa, I can't remember, I think the name of the place that the dances were given was the Pine Tree Inn, but I'm not sure about that. And in Abita Springs, it was the town pavilion, and it was right close to the famous real Abita Springs. In other words, the dance hall was right above the springs. You could walk down from the dance hall to the springs.
And what's famous about those springs, anyway?
Well, it's supposed to be the purest water in this part of the country, very healthful. People would go there to drink this water, and it was quite a health resort back in those days.
That's very restful over there. That's funny that you go there and you relax and everything. I don't know why it is.
Well, it's very restful country, pine country over there.
See, I asked you about Leonard Parker and Dan Moody. You don't remember them?
I don't remember them. No, I don't.
Black Eagle Vels there. You don't remember them? Those are people George Lewis has mentioned to me, playing over there. Who are some of the people you heard here in town?

Well, I was going to say, just about that time in New Orleans, of course this was, I suppose, the golden era of jazz around this part of the country, because in New Orleans around that time you had bands like, well, of course you had P-Ron out of Tranchina's. You had the old Chris Kelly and the Tuxedo bands, Celestan's band, playing for dancers. You had the Halfway House Band, out of Chris Rabinstein's Halfway House. Well, shortly after that, the Owls at the West End Roof, and the Owls also at the Pontchartrain Rowing Club. Sam Organ was playing here in New Orleans also. You had some fine bands in the cabarets downtown. The Little Club, as an example, hired the best bands that could be found, and even imported some name bands at the time. You might recall hearing one of them on record, which was the Scranton Sirens, which was a band that the Dorses played in. That was probably one of the voice recordings that was actually made in New Orleans. And Johnny Tobin had a band at that time, I think, at the ringside, and he cut the other side of the record, as you recall. There was a good band at the Cadillac Cabaret, but I don't recall the name of it. But there was plenty of good music all around town. Shortly after that, there was a band that played for dances around town. I think very little has been said of. And that was the Princeton Rebellers. Did you ever hear of them?
I have heard of them. I think it was Pinky.

It was a small group with Pinky, Vidalgovich, of course. And it was, as I recall, some of the boys from the Owl Band, because Bill Padron, I think, was on trumpet, and Bert Peck played the piano. I don't recall the rest of them. It was a very fine little band, never recorded, but just played for dances around town.
I think that's a band that combined with the Owls or something.
Probably did, because it was several of the same personnel.
I forget, Pinky told me about it once.
Pinky could give you the story on that, though.
He's one of the ones, isn't he?

And so, you might be interested in knowing some of the places that these dances were given, in addition to private homes, of course. Or places like the Audubon Tea Room, Tulane Gym, the Cartier Club. Have you heard of it? Never have.
How do you spell that?

I don't know. I have it, Q-U-A-R-T-I-E-R, that's what it sounds like. And I don't recall the exact spelling, but it was in the quarter, right around Jackson Square in that neighborhood. Never heard of it. Then there were dances given at the old Sazerac Bar, which was on Royal Street. I'll mention the Audubon Tea Room, of course. But there were many sororities and fraternities around town. And, you know, once you went to one of these dances, or several of them, you were almost automatically invited to others, and more or less the same group would be at these places.
The same kind of people being at the Cadillac that would be at the Audubon Tea Room?
Oh, no, no, I didn't mean that. No.
Well, I've tried to get a...

No, I meant the dances. I didn't... I wasn't referring to any clubs, nightclubs or cabarets. At that time, well, the youngsters didn't get around to those places too often. Money was scarce for one thing, and then... Wasn't quite the place to go for a lot of them.
Did Raymond ever tell you about that place? He never played there, but the band was behind Chicken Wire, so they wouldn't be hit by flying bottles. No, but I don't doubt it.
No, but I don't doubt it.
On Galliope Street. I don't doubt it.

There's one thing that I can remember very clearly. I can see him just like it was yesterday. And that was Santo Pecora. You know, he must have learned his instrument at a very early age, because I don't think he was more than 16 or 17 years old when he was playing with Joe Focco's band at the Old Palace. And he was taking solos and bringing down the house at that time. And I can recall very clearly.
Would Joe Focco let him play jazz at the Palace? Oh, yes. I always thought of him as a legit man. Well, he was.

As a matter of fact, my father gave me his first job in this town. But when you say jazz, it was not exactly a jazz band. It was, you might say, a show band. And they injected a little jazz into the... But it was certainly not a jazz band, no.
Joe Focco wasn't from New Orleans, or...?
I think, if I recall correctly, he was not born here. He came over from the old country. I think I'm correct in saying that.
Mm-hmm. Did you ever go to the original Two Bits Club?
No, don't recall that.
It's out by the lake. It's somewhere near West End. I'm trying to remember who told me about it. I think it was Bob Coquille told me about it. No. Red Mackey played there, somebody on that set.
The original Two Bits Club.
Did you know Red Mackey by any chance?

Yes, I knew Red, and his brother Dick. And, well, Dick was the trumpet player with the owl band that played at the rowing club, not the band that recorded. That's what I was trying to... The other band.
I got him confused. I was thinking of Dick. Yeah. And I said Red.
Yeah.
But you knew Dick too. Oh, yeah. What did he sound like?

Sounds very good. I don't know exactly whose style I would compare him with, but I think in those days that most of the young white carnet players were trying to get as close to Emmett Hardy as they could, so I suppose their style was a little like theirs.
Do you remember Hardy? Very vaguely.
Very vaguely. Very vaguely.
Did you hear him on this side of the river or the other side? No, this side.

I didn't know this side. Well, I think Monk Caswell can give you the pitch on Hardy probably better than anyone because of his connection, well, not only with Hardy but with the Boswell sisters because, as I recall it, Emmett and one of the Boswell girls were pretty friendly. And I know Monk was very friendly with the Boswells, so he probably knows that story better, as well as good as anyone. Want to cut it off? Alright.
You want to talk about the midnight shows now?

Well, I was thinking about the midnight shows at the Old Palace, I think it was, and the shows were, of course, for Negroes all during the week. It was a sort of a vaudeville circuit similar to the off-human circuits of that side except when it was Negroes. And each Friday night there was a midnight show for white people. And we, of course, tried never to miss it because, in addition to having a very good orchestra pit band, there were many good acts and good singers. I can recall hearing, for instance, Ethel Waters, Sarah Martin, Esther Bijou, some of the Smith sisters. There were so many of them. Not Bessie, of course. I didn't hear Bessie there, but I think Mamie Smith and some of the others. And there was a very fine drummer with this pit band. I don't recall his name.
What did he look like? Was he dark or light or...?
As I recall, rather on the short side and dark, yes. But I don't recall his name.
And which band was this at the minute?
This was Robichaud's band.
The fiddler or the piano player?
The fiddler. That's about all of that.
Paid? You mentioned paid dancers. You had dancers for your paid admission.
Oh, yes.
How much were they charged?
Well, even though... Are you speaking of the dancers on this side of the lake or on the other side?
Well, both, if you want to describe both.

Yeah, well, in most cases, the dancers were paid dancers. You paid so much per couple. To go in and to dance. Well, yes. Both this side and across the lake. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. How did prices run in the bars? Well, in many cases where the dancers were by invitation. Even though they were by invitation, it was... You paid so much per couple to go in and to dance.
Well, about what were the prices range?
Usually, two, two and a half, a couple.
That's across the lake? Well, yes.
Both this side and across the lake. Mm-hmm.
How did prices run in the bars?

Well, there were no bars in the dancers that I'm talking about. Remember, these were dancers that were given by, in most cases, private clubs and no bars. The bottle was out in the automobile and he went out during intermission and got a couple of slugs and... But, uh... They were never given... When I say they were given... For instance, I mentioned the old Sazerac bar. I didn't mean that that was a ballroom at the time that we gave these dancers. It had ceased to be a bar for quite some years and was rented out to individuals for parties and dances and whatnot. But we had no bar set up in these places at all. They either had a flask on your hip or a bottle in the automobile if you happened to have a car or something of that side. Now, in the cases, of course, in the case of Tranchinas and the Halfway House, well, those were nightclubs or cabarets or what have you. And, of course, you could buy a drink. But even in those places, in many cases, you brought your own bottle.
That was Prohibition Town. That's right. What were they selling?
God knows.
Well, would it be beer or wine or spirits or something? Well, yes.

Of course, this was many years ago. But I won't mention any names. But in many places, it wasn't supposed to sell whiskey. You could buy whiskey. It may be served in a demitasse coffee cup. But it was to be had in a great many places.
I guess, how would prices run, though, in those places? Like the Little Club or the Halfway House?

Well, now, I don't remember exactly. But in the case of the Little Club, I would say that it was probably the most expensive club in the city at that time. And demanded and got better prices than anywhere else. It was—they always came up with good talent and good bands and good entertainment, so they got the price.
Would it run a dollar and a half for a glass of gin or something? Or would it be fifty cents?
I don't recall. And I don't recall if you could buy whiskey in the club or not. It may have been that you had to bring your own. I don't recall that.
I think I've just about run out of questions, and we're about to run out of— Tape, too, huh?
Tape, too, yeah.
So we might as well close it off there.
Yeah.
Thank you very much, Joe. Let me just get this off. .
